title: A spiral needs a deflecting force carried by the growing body, not an external one

fields.label: Label
fields.value: A spiral needs a deflecting force carried by the growing body, not an external one

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: A deflecting force of constant direction acting from outside, such as wind or gravity, can only bend a growing structure towards a limiting direction and never into a spiral; a spiral arises only when the deflecting force is intrinsic to the growing body and turns with the direction of growth, as the columellar muscle does in the snail-shell.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the growing curve will tend to wind round and round its point of origin. In the typical case of the snail-shell, such an intrinsic force is manifestly present in the action of the columellar muscle.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XI, “The Logarithmic Spiral”; topic “Forces producing a spiral”. Scope: spirally growing shells and other growing structures subject to deflecting forces

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch11-02: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.46

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The fixed-versus-body-frame distinction is formalizable, but morphology alone cannot recover force direction. Existing shell scans are inadequate to identify the proposed columellar-muscle mechanism without new developmental or mechanical measurements.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Model and compare growing structures under fixed laboratory-frame versus body-rotating deflection fields, then test whether shell growth orientation and columellar-muscle geometry predict the observed spiral. A stable spiral under a demonstrably external fixed-direction force would refute necessity.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Multiple intrinsic growth asymmetries can mimic muscle deflection.

Growth-force direction is rarely measured in existing datasets.

The mathematical necessity depends on idealized force assumptions.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: That a fixed external direction cannot wind a growing structure into a spiral is a kinematic argument, not a dataset result. The biological claim that the co-rotating force is the columellar muscle needs measurements that have not been archived. Shell collections can show that spirals exist and cannot show which force produced them or exclude other intrinsic growth asymmetries.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: The empirical residue is whether a force that turns with the growing body, identified with the columellar muscle in snails, is what produces the spiral, as opposed to an external field of constant direction. That requires force or muscle-activity measurements during growth, not shell outline alone.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
No public dataset records muscle force through shell coiling.

Shell shape is compatible with any intrinsic asymmetry of growth and does not identify the columellar muscle as the deflecting force.
